questions.text: You just started your first job and earn £2,000/month before deductions. What does 'gross pay' mean?
questions.explanation: Gross pay is your total earnings before any deductions like tax or National Insurance.
questions.tip: Always compare your gross vs net pay so you understand where your money is going.

questions.text: You receive £1,600 in your bank after deductions. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Net pay is what you receive after deductions like tax and National Insurance.
questions.tip: Your net pay is what you should base your budget on—not your gross salary.

questions.text: Why do you pay income tax?
questions.explanation: Income tax funds public services like healthcare, education, and infrastructure.
questions.tip: Understanding taxes helps you avoid confusion when your take-home pay changes.

questions.explanation: A pension is a long-term savings plan to support you financially in retirement.
questions.tip: Start contributing early—even small amounts grow significantly over time.

questions.text: What is the first step in creating a budget?
questions.explanation: Tracking income and expenses helps you understand where your money goes.
questions.tip: Use apps or notes to track spending daily—it builds awareness fast.

questions.text: Your payslip shows deductions for 'NI'. What does this stand for?
questions.explanation: National Insurance contributions fund benefits like the NHS and state pension.
questions.tip: Check your payslip regularly so you understand all deductions, not just tax.

questions.text: Your employer matches your pension contributions. Why is this beneficial?
questions.explanation: Employer contributions increase your retirement savings without extra cost to you.
questions.tip: Always contribute enough to get full employer matching—it's essentially free money.

questions.text: You spend more than you earn each month. What is the likely outcome?
questions.explanation: Spending more than your income leads to debt accumulation over time.
questions.tip: If you're overspending, start by reducing small daily expenses—they add up quickly.

questions.text: What is a tax code on your payslip used for?
questions.explanation: A tax code determines how much income tax should be deducted from your salary.
questions.tip: If your tax code looks wrong, contact HMRC—you might be overpaying tax.

questions.text: Why is it important to start saving early for retirement?
questions.explanation: Starting early allows your savings to grow more through compound interest.
questions.tip: Time matters more than amount—starting early beats saving more later.

answers.text: Your money has more time to grow

questions.text: You earn £35,000/year and receive a £5,000 bonus. The higher tax rate starts at £37,700. How is your bonus taxed?
questions.explanation: Only income above £37,700 is taxed at the higher rate. So part of your bonus is taxed higher, not all of it.
questions.tip: Don’t fear bonuses—being in a higher tax band doesn’t mean all your income is taxed more.

answers.text: All £5,000 is taxed at the higher rate
Only the portion above £37,700 is taxed higher
None of the bonus is taxed

questions.text: You contribute 5% of your £2,400 monthly salary to your pension, and your employer contributes 3%. How much goes into your pension each month?
questions.explanation: 5% of £2,400 = £120 and 3% = £72, so £192 total goes into your pension monthly.
questions.tip: Use simple percentage calculations to quickly understand where your money is going.

questions.text: You save £300/month with 5% annual compound interest. After a few years, why does your balance grow faster even if you don’t increase contributions?
questions.explanation: Compound interest means you earn interest on both your savings and previously earned interest.
questions.tip: Start saving early—even small amounts benefit massively from compound growth.

questions.text: Your monthly income is £2,000. Fixed costs are £1,300 and variable spending is £600. What is the main financial risk?
questions.explanation: You only have £100 left, which creates a very small safety buffer for emergencies.
questions.tip: Aim to save at least 10–20% of your income to build a financial safety net.

answers.text: You have a very low financial buffer

questions.text: Your payslip shows a tax code change and higher deductions this month. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: A tax code change can adjust how much tax is deducted, especially if HMRC updates your records.
questions.tip: Always check changes in your payslip—small errors over time can cost you a lot.

answers.text: Your employer made a random error
Your tax code has been updated
